To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the distribution of biogenic facies within fjords of the Antarctic Peninsula is controlled by bay morphology and oceanography; (2) climate plays a secondary role, but along with ice drainage area, controls the rate and type of terrigenous supply; and (3) fjords along the Antarctic Peninsula with a high length-to-width ratio tend to have arenaceous sediments at the bottom where ice-rafted material is released preferentially in the head of the bay.

the distribution of biogenic sediments in the Antarctic Peninsula and the South Shetlend Islands is controlled by the geometry of the bay and oceanographic regime, and that climate controls the rate of ice-rafted sediment supply to the glaical marine environment.
fjord sedimentary facies are controlled by bay geometry, oceanographic regime, and climate, with the relative influence of each factor varying with location.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the processes that determine the nature of modern sedimentation in the Antarctic fjords and how the distribution of facies can be used to interpret past environmental conditions.
the physical processes that control the modern distribution of sediment types within fjord systems.
the processes that influence sedimentation within fjord systems and how these processes vary with climate, ice drainage basin size and oceanographic regime.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fjords along the Antarctic Peninsula have a variety of bottom sediments that reflect the interplay of oceanographic and physiographical controls on sediment transport and deposition.
the sedimentary facies within fjords are controlled by bay geometry, oceanographic regime, ice drainage basin size and climate.
the sediment distribution within fjords is controlled primarily by oceanographic and physiography factors and only secondarily by climate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sedimentary facies of Antarctic fjords are a function of fjord geometry, ice drainage basin size and oceanographic regime.

the sedimentary record of the last deglaciation and Holocene in the Antarctic Peninsula region will reflect a complex response to climate change and the interplay between oceanographic and physiographical controls on the glacial marine system.
the distribution of biogenic facies within the Antarctic fjords is controlled principally by the geometry of a fjord and its oceanographic regime, with climate playing a secondary role.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of biogenic sediments is controlled by the geometry of the fjord system, not the local climate.
the sedimentary facies in Antarctic fjords are not simply a function of climate.
the oceanographic and physical controls on sedimentation in the fjords of the Antarctic Peninsula have remained relatively constant over the last 10,000 years.
